title: The Assassination of Abraham Lincoln
context: President Abraham Lincoln was shot by the actor John Wilkes Booth at Ford's Theatre in Washington on the night of April 14, 1865, five days after Lee's surrender at Appomattox, and died the next morning. The same night Lewis Powell attacked Secretary of State William Seward at his home. Booth was cornered and killed at a Virginia farm on April 26. News moved by telegraph, so many papers printed bulletins in the order they arrived, including rumours later corrected.
reading_notes: Watch how certainty changes from bulletin to bulletin, and how Northern and Southern-leaning papers frame the conspiracy. Spellings of names (e.g. 'Payne' for Powell, who used that alias) differ from modern usage.
questions: How did papers first report the attack on Seward?
When was Booth's death reported, and how?
How was the funeral train described?

title: The Great Chicago Fire
context: Fire broke out on Chicago's West Side on the night of October 8, 1871, and burned until October 10, destroying about 3.3 square miles of the city, including the business district. Roughly 300 people died and around 100,000 were left homeless. Relief poured in from other cities, and the story of Mrs. O'Leary's cow, never proven, spread through the press.
reading_notes: Early casualty and loss figures were guesses and vary widely between papers. The O'Leary cow story is a useful case study in how a press rumour becomes 'fact'.
questions: How did papers explain the cause of the fire?
What relief efforts did other cities organize?
How did estimates of the losses change over the month?

title: The Johnstown Flood
context: On May 31, 1889, the South Fork Dam on the Little Conemaugh River in Pennsylvania failed after days of heavy rain, sending a wall of water down the valley onto Johnstown. More than 2,200 people died. The dam held back a lake owned by the South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club, whose members included wealthy Pittsburgh industrialists, and the press debated their responsibility. Clara Barton led one of the American Red Cross's first major relief operations there.
reading_notes: Death tolls in the first week range from hundreds to many thousands. Compare how papers treat the club's liability and the relief effort.
questions: Who did papers blame for the dam failure?
How was the Red Cross relief work reported?
How did the reported death toll change?

title: The Wright Brothers' First Flights
context: On December 17, 1903, Orville and Wilbur Wright made the first sustained, controlled flights of a powered heavier-than-air airplane at Kill Devil Hills near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. They flew four times that day; the longest flight, by Wilbur, covered 852 feet in 59 seconds. Press coverage was thin and often wrong: an embellished wire story spread from Norfolk, and many editors doubted the claims for years.
reading_notes: This collection is a lesson in how a world-changing event can be under-reported or misreported. Compare reported distances and details with the Wrights' own account.
questions: How far did newspapers say the machine flew?
Which papers were sceptical?
How did the Wrights' statement correct the press?

title: The 1906 San Francisco Earthquake and Fire
context: At 5:12 a.m. on April 18, 1906, a major earthquake on the San Andreas Fault struck San Francisco. Fires that followed burned for several days and destroyed most of the city. Official death counts at the time were in the hundreds; later research puts the toll at roughly 3,000 or more. More than half of the city's roughly 400,000 residents were left homeless.
reading_notes: Early reports undercounted deaths, partly to protect the city's reputation and partly because of chaos. Note what the press says about martial law, looting and the army's use of dynamite.
questions: How were the fires fought?
What did papers report about looting and martial law?
How did other cities send aid?

title: The Sinking of the Titanic
context: The White Star liner Titanic struck an iceberg at about 11:40 p.m. on April 14, 1912, on her maiden voyage, and sank about 2 hours 40 minutes later. Around 1,500 people died; about 700 survivors were picked up by the Cunard liner Carpathia, which reached New York on the night of April 18. The first wireless reports were confused, and some papers on April 15 reported that all passengers were safe and the ship was being towed to Halifax.
reading_notes: Compare the early 'all saved' reports with those from April 16 onward. Survivor lists were printed and reprinted with many spelling errors. US Senate hearings began on April 19.
questions: When did papers first report the loss of life?
What did survivors say about the lifeboats?
How was the Carpathia's arrival reported?

title: The Sinking of the Lusitania
context: On May 7, 1915, the German submarine U-20 torpedoed the Cunard liner Lusitania off the south coast of Ireland. She sank in about 18 minutes, and 1,198 people died, among them 128 Americans. The sinking turned much American opinion against Germany, though the United States did not enter the war until April 1917. Germany argued the ship carried munitions and had published warnings to travellers.
reading_notes: Read for editorial positions on neutrality and for the German embassy's newspaper warning, which some papers reprinted.
questions: How did American papers react to the sinking?
What was said about the German warning notice?
How did President Wilson respond?

title: The 1918 Influenza Pandemic
context: The deadliest wave of the 1918-1919 influenza pandemic hit the United States in autumn 1918, peaking in October. Cities closed schools, churches, theaters and saloons, banned public gatherings and urged masks, with very different timing and strictness. Around 675,000 Americans died over the whole pandemic, and estimates of deaths worldwide run to about 50 million. Wartime censorship shaped reporting in many countries.
reading_notes: Look for closure orders, advertisements for remedies, and how local officials played down or played up the danger. 'Spanish influenza' was the common name; Spain was neutral and its press reported the disease openly.
questions: What public-health orders did cities issue?
Which remedies were advertised?
How did officials describe the danger?

title: The Armistice of November 1918
context: The armistice ending fighting on the Western Front was signed early on November 11, 1918, in a railway carriage in the forest of Compiègne, and took effect at 11 a.m. Paris time. Four days earlier, on November 7, a premature United Press report that an armistice had been signed set off celebrations across the United States before it was denied.
reading_notes: Compare the 'false armistice' coverage of November 7-8 with the real news of November 11. Look at how the terms were summarized for readers.
questions: How was the false armistice reported and then corrected?
What terms did papers say Germany accepted?
How were celebrations described?

title: Ratification of the 19th Amendment
context: On August 18, 1920, Tennessee became the 36th state to ratify the 19th Amendment, giving it the three-quarters of states needed to bar denial of the vote on account of sex. The deciding vote in the Tennessee House came from 24-year-old Harry Burn, who changed his vote after a letter from his mother. Opponents tried to reverse the vote, but Secretary of State Bainbridge Colby certified the amendment on August 26, 1920.
reading_notes: Many Black women, especially in the South, remained kept from voting by poll taxes, literacy tests and violence long after 1920. Watch for whose voices the coverage includes.
questions: How was Harry Burn's vote reported?
What did opponents try after the vote?
When could women first vote in the 1920 election?

title: Lindbergh's Transatlantic Flight
context: Charles Lindbergh took off from Roosevelt Field, Long Island, on May 20, 1927, and landed at Le Bourget, near Paris, on the evening of May 21, about 33 and a half hours later. It was the first solo nonstop flight across the Atlantic, and it won the $25,000 Orteig Prize. His plane was the Spirit of St. Louis. He became an instant celebrity, and newspapers covered his return to the United States in June at enormous length.
reading_notes: A study in mass-media celebrity. Compare factual flight reports with human-interest coverage of Lindbergh's mother and the crowds in Paris.
questions: How was the landing in Paris described?
What did Lindbergh say about the flight?
How was his return welcomed?

title: The Stock Market Crash of 1929
context: Prices on the New York Stock Exchange fell sharply on Thursday, October 24, 1929 ('Black Thursday'), when leading bankers organized buying to steady the market, and collapsed again on Monday, October 28, and Tuesday, October 29 ('Black Tuesday'), when about 16 million shares changed hands. The crash wiped out paper fortunes and is often taken as the start of the Great Depression, though historians stress that its causes and effects were broader.
reading_notes: Watch how officials and business leaders reassured the public, and how quickly papers called the worst over. Ticker delays meant readers often learned prices hours late.
questions: What did bankers do on October 24?
How did officials reassure investors?
How were small investors affected?

title: Bombay's English Press, 1811-1930
context: A sample of about three issues per decade from four Bombay newspapers held in the Internet Archive's IndiaHistory collection: the Bombay Courier, The Bombay Gazette, The Bombay Guardian and The Bombay Chronicle. Together they cover more than a century of the city, from an East India Company port to the commercial capital of British India. They span the cotton boom of the 1860s, the plague that struck Bombay from 1896, the 1918 influenza and the rise of the nationalist movement, which The Bombay Chronicle (founded 1910) championed. The full runs total almost 30,000 issues. Use the India archive page to search inside all of them.
reading_notes: These were papers of the colonial and commercial elite, mostly British-owned until the Chronicle. Much of each issue is advertising, shipping lists, government notices and reprinted European news. Indian voices appear chiefly in letters, court reports and, later, the nationalist press. The OCR comes from a modern engine running over old microfilm, so expect noise in small type and tables. Only issues published before 1931 are copied here.
questions: plague deaths in Bombay
cotton prices and the American war
What did papers say about the Indian National Congress?
shipping arrivals from London

title: Calcutta's English Press, 1819-1891
context: Calcutta was the capital of British India until 1911 and the centre of its press. The Calcutta Journal (1818-1823) was founded by James Silk Buckingham, who was deported for criticizing the East India Company's government. The Hindoo Patriot, founded in 1853, was one of the leading Indian-run English weeklies. Its 1875-1891 issues here cover the Vernacular Press Act of 1878, the Ilbert Bill controversy of 1883 and the founding of the Indian National Congress in 1885.
reading_notes: The Calcutta Journal wrote for the European community and its quarrels with the Company. The Hindoo Patriot spoke for educated, propertied Bengalis and often criticized the government while professing loyalty to the Crown. Both reprint much from London papers.
questions: Ilbert Bill
Vernacular Press Act
Indian National Congress
East India Company and the liberty of the press

title: The Indian-Language Press in Translation, 1868-1916
context: From the 1860s, provincial governments in British India had translators read the Indian-language press every week and report, in English, what each paper was saying, often quoting it at length. These 'Selections from the Vernacular Newspapers' (now Indian Newspaper Reports, held at the British Library) let you hear hundreds of Hindi, Urdu, Bengali, Marathi, Gujarati, Tamil and other newspapers that were never digitized, on famine, taxation, religion, the Vernacular Press Act, the partition of Bengal, the First World War and the national movement. The sample here runs from 1868 to 1916; later reports are searchable from the India archive page.
reading_notes: These are surveillance documents: the government chose what to translate and how, and they over-represent criticism it worried about. Each entry names the original paper, its place and date, so cite both the report and the paper it summarizes. Translation can soften or sharpen the original's tone.
questions: What did vernacular papers say about the famine?
partition of Bengal
Vernacular Press Act
Tilak

title: Indian-Language Press: Tamil and Telugu, 1850-1930
context: Tamil newspapers and periodicals from the 1850s to 1930, such as Narpotakam, Janavinotini, Arunotayam and others, digitized through the British Library's Endangered Archives Programme. Alongside them are 1930 issues of Zamin Ryot, a Telugu weekly from Nellore. Indian-language papers reached far more readers than the English press and carried debates on religion, social reform, education and politics in their readers' own languages.
reading_notes: Search in Tamil or Telugu script. OCR for Indian scripts on old type is noisy: conjunct letters and vowel signs are often misread, so try several forms of a word. Many periodicals were monthly or irregular, and dates in titles are sometimes approximate.
questions: கல்வி
காந்தி
రైతు
ప్రభుత్వం

title: Gazettes of India Through Time, 1920s-2020s

india_samples.name: State and provincial gazettes

context: About three gazette issues per decade from the 1920s to the 2020s: the Gazette of India (weekly and extraordinary issues, before and after independence) and state gazettes such as Haryana's, Tamil Nadu's and Karnataka's. Gazettes are where government becomes law: they carry acts and ordinances, appointments, land acquisitions, notices of lost securities, name changes and public notices. The Internet Archive's gazetteofindia collection, digitized by Public.Resource.Org, holds over 877,000 issues. Use the India archive page to search inside all of them.
reading_notes: Gazettes are formal legal records and often bilingual (English with Hindi or a state language). Tables and lists OCR poorly. The issue date is the date of publication, which is not always when a notification took effect. Citations point to the issue; open it at the Internet Archive to find the page.
questions: land acquisition notification
appointment of judges
change of name notice
famine relief

title: Indian Headlines, August 2020
context: Headlines from 87 Indian news outlets, from The Times of India, The Hindu and The Indian Express to NDTV, Mint, Scroll.in and regional papers such as the Deccan Herald, The Tribune and The Sentinel. They were collected for this project's first version, almost all between 1 and 18 August 2020 (a few dozen older items came along). India was then in the 'Unlock 3' phase of easing its COVID-19 lockdown, and reported cases passed two million in early August. Other stories of that fortnight include the foundation-stone ceremony for the Ram temple in Ayodhya on 5 August, the Air India Express crash at Kozhikode on 7 August, and the violence in Bengaluru on 11 August.
reading_notes: These are headlines only, with a link to each article; the article text is not stored, so open the link to read the story. Each record carries the topic the aggregator assigned (Nation, World, Business, Health and so on), which is not always the outlet's own section. Many outlets ran the same agency copy (PTI, ANI, IANS) under different headlines, and online headlines are written to be clicked. Some links may have moved or gone behind paywalls since 2020.
questions: How did Indian outlets cover COVID-19 vaccine trials?
What was reported about the Kozhikode plane crash?
Ayodhya Ram temple bhoomi pujan
How did the business press report the economy and RBI?

title: The Gazette of India, 30 September 2000

ia_item_fields.newspaper: The Gazette of India, Part III, Section 4
ia_item_fields.rights: Government of India publication, digitized by Public.Resource.Org and the Internet Archive (gazetteofindia collection).

context: The Gazette of India is the Government of India's official journal of record, published in Hindi and English. Laws, rules, appointments and public notices take legal effect by appearing in it. This weekly issue's Part III, Section 4 carries 'Miscellaneous Notifications including Notifications, Orders, Advertisements and Notices issued by Statutory Bodies'. Here that means notices from the Reserve Bank of India and public-sector banks, such as lists of government securities reported lost under the Public Debt Act, 1944, and bank regulations on staff taking private employment after retirement. It is the issue the first version of this project scraped. This copy comes from the Internet Archive, whose OCR reads both the English and the Hindi pages.
reading_notes: A gazette is a legal record, not a newspaper. Notices are formal and repetitive, and long tables (lists of securities, names and addresses) come out of OCR as broken fragments. The Hindi and English versions of a notice often appear side by side, so search in either language. Citations point to the issue; use the Internet Archive viewer to find the page.
questions: Which securities were reported lost to the Reserve Bank of India?
Rules on bank officers taking private employment after retirement
सेवानिवृत्ति के पश्चात् निजी क्षेत्र में नियोजन
State Bank of India appointment of managing director
